title: The image tax
context: A developer asked an AI assistant to add a hero banner image to a Next.js landing page. The suggested code renders the image correctly, but the Lighthouse performance score drops sharply and the Largest Contentful Paint time nearly triples.
question: Why does this hero image tank the page's Largest Contentful Paint score?
options: A plain ships the full-resolution source file with no responsive sizing, lazy-loading, or modern format conversion — next/image handles all of that automatically and this code opts out of it.
Next.js blocks all tags from rendering above the fold by default.
Long alt text forces the browser to delay paint until it's been read.
<section> elements can't contain images without an explicit width and height in Next.js.

explanation.theBug: A plain img tag serves the source file exactly as it is — full resolution, original format, no lazy-loading hints, and the browser doesn't know its dimensions ahead of time, which can also cause layout shift. Next.js ships next/image specifically to solve this: automatic resizing per device, modern format conversion like WebP or AVIF, and priority loading hints for above-the-fold images. Using a raw img for a large hero image opts out of all of it, and the unoptimized file becomes the single biggest resource blocking Largest Contentful Paint.
explanation.whyAIGeneratesThis: A plain img tag is the universal, framework-agnostic way to render an image in HTML, and it's what most training data outside of Next.js-specific examples uses. The model doesn't reliably default to a framework-specific optimized component unless the prompt explicitly mentions performance or Next.js image handling — plain HTML is the safe, generic answer it falls back on.

theFix.commentary: next/image handles responsive sizing and format conversion automatically; priority tells Next.js to preload this specific image since it's above the fold.

explanation.reviewHeuristic: In a Next.js codebase, treat every raw img tag as worth a second look — is next/image intentionally skipped here, or did the AI just default to generic HTML?
